question: A Monster object has a name and a health value, and it can roar and take damage. In object-oriented terms, which is which?
correct: name and health are its state (fields); roar and takeDamage are its behavior (methods)
incorrect: name and health are its behavior (methods); roar and takeDamage are its state (fields)
All four are state, because all four of them belong to the one Monster object
All four are behavior, because all four of them are written inside the Monster class
feedback: An object bundles two things. Its state is what it KNOWS: the data kept in its fields, such as a name and a health value. Its behavior is what it can DO: its methods, such as roar() and takeDamage(). Keeping the two together is the whole idea: a monster carries its own health and knows how to lose some of it.

question: A {{1}} is a blueprint: it says what fields and methods every Monster will have. An {{2}}, also called an instance, is one actual Monster built from that blueprint, and it is made with the keyword {{3}}.
feedback: A class is written once and describes a kind of thing. Objects are made from it, as many as you like, each by a new expression: Monster goblin = new Monster(); Monster dragon = new Monster(); is one class and two objects. The class is the plan; the objects are the monsters.

question:
Complete the line so that it creates a Dog object and runs the Dog constructor:
Dog rex = ___ Dog("Rex");
correct: new
feedback: new creates the object and runs the constructor; rex then holds a reference to the finished object. Leave the word out and the line does not compile, because Dog("Rex") on its own looks like a call to a method named Dog. Declaring just  Dog rex;  creates no object at all: a local variable written that way has no value yet (the compiler will not let you read it), and a field written that way holds null.

question: Two objects are made from one class, and their fields are set with a dot. What does this print?
feedback: goblin.health means “the health field of the object goblin refers to”. Each Monster made with new has fields of its own, so taking 5 from the goblin leaves the dragon at 200. The class is one blueprint; the objects are two separate monsters.

question: Two Counter objects are created from the same class. What does the program print?
feedback: count is an instance field, so each object made with new carries its own copy. new ran twice, which makes two objects and two separate counts: a's is raised twice and b's once. Nothing done to one object reaches the other.

question: You are writing a Hero class for a game. Match each kind of variable to the piece of data it suits.

pairs.definition: One hero's current hit points, remembered between method calls
A running total needed only while one method adds up a hero's loot
The amount of damage a caller hands to takeDamage(...)

feedback: Ask who owns the data and how long it has to live. Data that each object must remember belongs in a field: it stays for as long as the object does, and every method of the class can use it. A value needed only during one method call is a local variable, gone when the method returns. A value the caller supplies for that call is a parameter.

question: A method can use and change the fields of the object it is called on. What does this print?
feedback: Inside takeDamage, health means the health of whichever monster the method was called on: here, the orc. The field is not a local variable, so it does not vanish when the method ends: after the first call it holds 50, and the second call starts from there and leaves 25.

correct: Once for each new Potion(...) expression, as that object is being created
incorrect: Once when the program starts, before main, to prepare the Potion class
Each time a method is called on a Potion, so that its fields are set first
Once, for the first Potion; later Potions reuse the values it set up
feedback: Potion(int doses) is a constructor: it has the class's name and no return type, and Java runs it as part of every new Potion(...). Three new expressions mean three separate runs, each filling in the fields of a different object. It is not a start-up routine for the class, it does not run again when you call methods on the object, and nothing is shared between one Potion and the next.

question: Which statements about constructors are true?
correct: A constructor has the same name as its class
A class may declare several constructors if their parameter lists differ
If a class declares no constructor, the compiler supplies one that takes no arguments
incorrect: A constructor is declared with the return type void, because it returns nothing
Java still supplies a no-argument constructor after you write one that takes parameters
A constructor can be called again on an existing object to reset it, as in rex.Dog("Max")
feedback: A constructor is named after its class and has NO return type at all. That matters: write  void Dog() { ... }  and it still compiles, but as an ordinary method that happens to be called Dog, so new Dog() never runs it and the fields keep their defaults. A class can have several constructors with different parameter lists. The free no-argument constructor exists only while you have written none: add Dog(String name) and  new Dog()  stops compiling. And a constructor runs only as part of new; rex.Dog("Max") is not legal, so resetting an object is a job for a method.

question:
Put in order, first to last, what happens when Java runs this line:
Dog rex = new Dog("Rex");
items: Memory is set aside for one new Dog object
The new object's fields are filled with default values
The constructor body runs and assigns the fields
A reference to the finished object is stored in rex
feedback: The right-hand side is finished before the assignment happens. new first makes room for the object and fills its fields with defaults, which is why a constructor that forgets a field leaves 0, false or null behind. Then the constructor body runs. Only when the object is complete does = store a reference to it in rex.

question: NPC: The assignment that does nothing
intro: Zoya the Golem-Shaper sets a small clay golem on the bench. It does not move. “Seven runes of power I gave it,” they say, “and it has none. Read my class with me.”

steps.say: Every golem I shape is one object, and the class Golem says each object has a field called power. Inside the constructor there are TWO things named power: the parameter and the field. When a name could mean either, the nearer one wins, so plain power means the parameter.

beats.say: Every golem I shape is one object. The class says each Golem object has a field called power.
Inside the constructor there are TWO things named power: the parameter and the field. The nearer one wins, so plain power means the parameter. We say the parameter shadows the field.

steps.say: So  power = power;  copies the parameter into itself. The field is never touched — and a field nobody assigns keeps its default value. For an int field that default is 0.

wrong: Nothing — the class does not compile
check.why: It compiles fine, which is what makes this bug nasty. The 7 was copied onto itself and thrown away; the field still holds its default, 0.

steps.say: The cure is the keyword this, which means the object being built right now. this.power is that object's field; plain power is still the parameter. Defaults to remember: number fields start at 0, boolean fields at false, and fields that refer to objects, such as a String, start at null.

beats.say: The cure is the keyword this. It means “the object being built right now”, so this.power is that object's field.
Keep the defaults in mind too: a number field starts at 0, a boolean field at false, and a field that refers to an object — a String, say — starts at null.

outro: “The next monster made my mistake with a String field. Decide what each field really holds before you answer.”

question: One of the two assignments in this constructor does nothing. What does the program print?
correct: null 5
feedback: Inside the constructor, name means the parameter, because the parameter shadows the field of the same name. name = name; copies the parameter onto itself, so the field keeps the default for a String field, null. The second assignment is fine: the parameter is called lvl, so level can only mean the field, which becomes 5. Writing this.name = name; fixes the bug.

question: A constructor has a parameter named hp, and its class has a field that is also named hp. Write the statement that stores the parameter in the field.
correct: this.hp = hp;
feedback: this.hp is the field of the object being built; plain hp is the parameter, because a parameter shadows a field with the same name. The field goes on the left since that is where the value is stored. hp = hp; compiles but changes nothing, and hp = this.hp; copies in the wrong direction, overwriting the parameter with the field's default.

question: This class has two constructors. What does the program print?
feedback: A class may have several constructors as long as they take different lists of values; that is called overloading. Java chooses by what is in the parentheses: three values run the first constructor, two values run the second, which sets the price to 0 itself. The stick still gets its own name and damage.

question: This class has two constructors, and one of them hands the work to the other. What does the program print?
feedback: Java picks the constructor whose parameter list matches the arguments. new Potion("Elixir") matches the one-parameter constructor, and this(name, 3) inside it runs the two-parameter constructor of the same class with doses = 3. q calls the two-parameter constructor directly with 5. Chaining with this(...) keeps the real set-up code in one place. (Older Java insisted that this(...) open the constructor; Java 25 allows other statements ahead of it, provided they do not use the object being built.)

question: A Monster's health field is NOT private. What can go wrong that making it private would prevent?
correct: Code in any other class can set it to a nonsense value such as -999
incorrect: Two Monster objects would end up sharing one single health value
The Monster's own methods would be unable to change the health
The health value would be lost each time one of its methods ends
feedback: A field that is not private can be written by anyone: goblin.health = -999; compiles and runs, and the game's rules are broken. Making it private means the only way to change it is through the class's own methods, which can refuse a bad value. That is encapsulation. Objects never share a field of this kind, a class can always use its own fields, and a field lasts as long as its object.

question: A field or method marked {{1}} can be used only by code inside its own class. One marked {{2}} can be used by code in any class. One with no access modifier at all can be used by any class in the same {{3}}.
feedback: private is the tightest level and the normal choice for fields; public is the loosest and the normal choice for the methods other classes are meant to call. Leaving the modifier off gives package access: visible to the classes in the same package and to nobody else. A fourth level, protected, only makes sense once you have met inheritance.

question: Inside a class, declare a private int field named balance. Do not give it a starting value.
correct: private int balance;
feedback: The order is access modifier, then type, then name: private int balance;. Java rejects int private balance; and private balance int;. With no starting value the field begins at 0, the default for an int field.

correct: It does not compile: gold has private access in Vault
incorrect: It compiles, but throws an exception when the assignment runs
It compiles, but the assignment to gold is silently ignored
It compiles and stores 9999: private blocks code in other packages
feedback: private is enforced by the compiler, not while the program runs. Code outside Vault may not even mention v.gold, so the program is never built and there is nothing to throw an exception or to be ignored. Being in the same package does not help, because private means this class and no other. That is the point of encapsulation: the only way in is through the methods Vault chooses to offer.

question: A class Vault declares the field  private int gold;  Which statements about gold are true?
correct: Code in another class may not assign to it directly, even through a Vault variable
A method of Vault can read the gold of a different Vault object passed in as a parameter
incorrect: Its value can no longer be changed once the constructor has finished running
It is shared: every Vault object reads and writes the very same gold value
The class will not compile unless one of its constructors gives it a value
feedback: private controls WHO may touch a field, and nothing else. The boundary is the class, not the object, so a Vault method such as  boolean richerThan(Vault other)  may read other.gold. private does not freeze the value, does not make objects share it (each Vault still has a gold of its own), and does not oblige a constructor to set it.

question: The class Hero has the field  private int level;  Which method is a correctly written getter for it?
correct: public int getLevel() { return level; }
incorrect: public void getLevel() { System.out.println(level); }
public int getLevel(int level) { return level; }
public void getLevel() { return level; }
feedback: A getter RETURNS the field, so its return type is the field's type and it needs no parameters. Printing is not returning: the void version shows the number on the screen, but the caller cannot store it or compare it. The version with a parameter hands back whatever the caller passed in, because the parameter shadows the field. A void method that tries to return a value does not compile.

question: A {{1}} hands back the value of a private field and usually takes no parameters. A {{2}} takes one parameter, may check it before storing it, and usually has the return type {{3}}.
feedback: A getter (or accessor) reads: its return type matches the field and it needs no input. A setter (or mutator) writes: it receives the new value as a parameter, and since it has nothing to report back its return type is normally void. Because every change has to pass through the setter, the class gets the chance to refuse values that make no sense.

question: NPC: A setter that says no
intro: Zoya's kiln glows in the corner of the workshop. “An apprentice once set this to five thousand degrees,” they say. “Once. Then I rewrote the class.”

steps.say: heat is private, so no outside code can write k.heat = 5000. The only way in is the setter, and the setter looks at the new value before storing it. Checking a value before accepting it is called validation.

beats.say: Here is my Kiln class. The field heat is private, so no outside code can write k.heat = 5000.
The only way in is the setter, setHeat, and it looks at the new value before storing it. Checking a value before you accept it is called validation.

steps.say: Two calls: one sensible, one not.

beats.say: A new Kiln k starts at 200. Then two calls arrive: one sensible, one not.

check.why: 650 passes the if, so it is stored. 5000 fails it, the assignment is skipped, and the field keeps the last good value.

steps.say: A rejected value leaves the field exactly as it was. That is what encapsulation buys you: a private field plus a validating setter means the object can never hold a nonsense value, whoever calls it.

outro: “The next monster's setter guards a hero's hit points. Take the calls one at a time and ask each: does this value get in?”

question: This setter validates the new value before storing it. What does the program print?
feedback: Take the calls one at a time. 120 is above 100, so the if is false and hp stays 10. 45 is inside the range, so hp becomes 45. -5 is below 0, so it is refused and hp stays 45. The last call is not automatically the winner: only values that pass validation are stored.

feedback_template: balance starts at 100. deposit({{a}}) passes its check, giving {{mid}}. deposit(-{{b}}) fails amount > 0 and is ignored. withdraw({{w}}) is positive and no more than the balance, so it goes through and leaves {{expected}}. withdraw(500) asks for more than the account holds, so it is refused and the balance stays at {{expected}}.

question: Which statements about getters and setters are true?
correct: A setter can refuse a bad value and leave the field as it was
A getter may compute what it returns, such as a full name built from two fields
A class may give a field a getter and deliberately leave out the setter
incorrect: A private field with a getter can be assigned from outside, as in h.getHp() = 5;
A setter has to be named set plus the field name, or the class will not compile
feedback: Getters and setters are ordinary methods, so they can contain any logic. A setter can validate; a getter can simply return the field (most do) or build its answer, as in return first + " " + last;. A field with a getter and no setter is read-only from outside, which is often exactly what you want. A getter hands back a copy of the value, not the field itself, so h.getHp() = 5; does not compile. The names getHp and setHp are a convention people and tools rely on; the compiler does not care.

question: A Hero is handed Item objects. What does the program print?
feedback: The hero starts with 50. The potion costs 20, which the hero can afford: 30 left. The sword costs 40, more than 30, so the if is false and nothing changes. A second potion goes through: 10 left. The Hero never looks inside the Item; it asks the item for its price, each time, through getPrice().

question: price is a private field of Item. Inside Hero's method  buy(Item item),  how does the hero find out what the item costs?
correct: By calling item.getPrice(), a public method of Item
incorrect: By reading item.price, since buy was handed the item
By reading this.price, since the hero now owns the item
It cannot: a private field is hidden from all objects
feedback: private means “only code inside Item may touch this”, and buy is code inside Hero, so item.price does not compile, whoever the item was handed to. this.price would be a field of the HERO, which has none. The way in is the one Item offers: its public getter. Objects work together by calling each other's methods.

question: Which line makes a list that can hold Monster objects?
correct: ArrayList<Monster> monsters = new ArrayList<>();
incorrect: ArrayList<monsters> Monster = new ArrayList<>();
Monster[] monsters = new ArrayList<Monster>();
ArrayList monsters = new Monster<ArrayList>();
feedback: The angle brackets say what the list holds, and a class of your own can go there just as String or Integer can: ArrayList<Monster>. The variable's name comes after the type. A Monster[] is an array, a different thing, and it is the ArrayList that is made with new, not the Monster.

question: A list of objects, walked with a for-each loop. What does this print?
feedback: Each add puts one new Monster in the list, so its size is 3. In the loop, m is each monster in turn, and m.getHealth() asks that monster for its own health: 30 + 60 + 200 = 290. A new Monster can be made right inside add(…); it does not need a variable of its own.

correct: Dog@1b6d3586
incorrect: Rex
rex
Dog: Rex
feedback: println asks the object for its toString(). A class that writes none gets a basic one: the class name, an @, and a code that says nothing about the fields (and varies from run to run). Java does not guess that name is the interesting field, and the object has no idea what its variable is called. To see something useful, the class has to write toString itself.

question: This class supplies its own toString. What does the program print?
correct: Elixir x3
feedback: println(p) calls p.toString() for you, and this class has replaced the basic Potion@... version with one that builds a readable string: name, then " x", then doses. The same call happens whenever an object is joined to a String with +. The @Override line asks the compiler to check that the method really does replace an existing one, so a slip such as tostring() is caught instead of silently ignored.

question: Monster writes a method  public String toString().  What does it mean to say that this OVERRIDES the default toString()?
correct: Monster's version replaces the default one, and is what runs
incorrect: Both versions run: the default one first, then Monster's
The default one still runs unless toString() is named
Monster's version runs only for the first Monster made
feedback: Every class starts out with a toString() that gives the class name and a code. Writing your own with exactly the same name, return type and (empty) parameter list replaces it: from then on, wherever Java needs a Monster as text, yours is the one that runs, for every Monster. Putting @Override above it asks the compiler to check that it really does replace something.

question: Monster's toString() returns  name + " [HP=" + health + "]".  monsters is an ArrayList holding a Goblin with 30 health and an Orc with 60. What does  System.out.println(monsters);  print?
correct: [Goblin [HP=30], Orc [HP=60]]
incorrect: [Monster@1b6d3586, Monster@4e25154f]
Goblin [HP=30] Orc [HP=60]
[Goblin, Orc]
feedback: A list prints itself as square brackets around its elements, separated by commas, and to show each element it calls that element's toString(). So each monster appears exactly as its own toString() describes it. Without a toString() in Monster, the list would show the default class-name-and-code for each one.

question: NPC: A test that tells a little story
intro: Zoya sets an unfinished clay figure on the bench, and beside it a short list of things to try on it. "A method could be tested by handing it numbers. An object cannot. What a method DID shows only in what the object has become."

steps.say: Each test makes an object, does something to it, and then looks at one thing.

beats.say: From here on, each row of the table is a little story: make an object, do something to it, then look at one thing.
The last line is what the test looks at. Everything above it is how the object got there.

check.prompt: A row reads  Monster a = new Monster("A", 30); Monster b = new Monster("B", 8); a.takeDamage(5); b.getHealth()  — what should it show?
check.why: The damage was done to a. b is a different object with a health of its own, and nothing touched it. A row like this is there to catch a class whose objects are not keeping their own data.

steps.say: Sometimes you write one method of a class that is given. Sometimes you write the whole class.

beats.say: First you will be handed a class that is nearly finished, and write one method of it. The class so far is shown above the box; read its fields before you start.
Later the box is the whole class: fields first, then a constructor, then the methods. The question says exactly what to call each one, because the tests will use those names.
Some rows only ask whether a field is private. As always: Run costs nothing, and only Submit counts.

outro: "Spelling counts here. If the question says getHealth, a method called gethealth is a method the tests cannot find."

question: Finish describe() so that it returns a sentence about THIS potion, built from its three fields, in the form  Health Potion restores 50 health and costs 10 gold.

tests.expect: Health Potion restores 50 health and costs 10 gold.
Mana Elixir restores 30 health and costs 15 gold.
A restores 0 health and costs 5 gold.

solution: return name + " restores " + healingAmount + " health and costs " + price + " gold.";
hint: Inside a method, the fields are used by their names: name, healingAmount and price. Join them to the fixed words with +.
feedback: A method uses the fields of the object it was called on, by their plain names. It RETURNS the sentence instead of printing it, so that whoever called it can decide what to do with the text.

question: Write the body of the constructor: store its two parameters in the fields that have the same names.

tests.run: Monster m = new Monster("Goblin", 30);
Monster m = new Monster("Goblin", 30);

Monster a = new Monster("Orc", 60);
Monster b = new Monster("Slime", 10);

hint: The parameters hide the fields of the same names. this.name is the field; plain name is the parameter.
feedback: Inside the constructor, name on its own means the parameter. this.name means the field of the object being built, so this.name = name; copies the one into the other. Writing name = name; compiles, copies the parameter onto itself, and leaves the field empty.

question: Finish takeDamage so that it lowers THIS monster's health by amount. Health must never go below 0.

tests.run:
Monster m = new Monster("Goblin", 30);
m.takeDamage(10);

Monster m = new Monster("Goblin", 30);
m.takeDamage(99);

hint: Subtract first. Then, if health has gone below 0, set it back to 0.
feedback: The method changes the object's own field, and nothing needs to be returned: the change is still there the next time anyone asks. The if is the class protecting its own data; no caller can make this monster's health negative.

question: Finish the setter. A damage from 0 to 100 is stored as it is. Anything below 0 is stored as 0, and anything above 100 is stored as 100.

tests.run:
Weapon w = new Weapon("Axe");
w.setDamage(60);

Weapon w = new Weapon("Dagger");
w.setDamage(-10);

Weapon w = new Weapon("Bow");
w.setDamage(150);

Weapon w = new Weapon("Spear");
w.setDamage(100);

hint: Three cases: too low, too high, and fine. An if / else if / else that assigns damage in each.
feedback: A setter is the one door into a private field, so it is the place to check what comes through. Here a bad value is pulled back to the nearest allowed one; the edges 0 and 100 are themselves allowed, which is why the tests are < 0 and > 100.

question: Finish buyItem. If the hero has enough gold, take the item's price off the gold and return  Aria buys Health Potion for 20 gold.  If not, leave the gold alone and return  Aria cannot afford Sword.

tests.run:
Hero hero = new Hero("Aria", 50);
Item potion = new Item("Health Potion", 20);
tests.expect: Aria buys Health Potion for 20 gold.

tests.run:
Hero hero = new Hero("Aria", 50);
hero.buyItem(new Item("Health Potion", 20));

Hero hero = new Hero("Aria", 10);
Item sword = new Item("Sword", 25);

Hero hero = new Hero("Aria", 10);
hero.buyItem(new Item("Sword", 25));

Hero hero = new Hero("Bo", 20);
hero.buyItem(new Item("Potion", 20));

hint: The item's fields are private. Ask it: item.getPrice() and item.getName(). “Enough” includes having exactly the price.
feedback: Two objects working together. The hero cannot read item.price, because that field is private to Item; it calls the getters Item offers instead. The hero's own gold is its own field, used by its plain name. Having exactly the price is enough, so the test is >=.

question: Write toString so that a monster is shown as its name and health in the form  Goblin [HP=30]

tests.run: Monster m = new Monster("Goblin", 30);
Monster m = new Monster("Dragon", 200);

hint: Return the text; do not print it. Join the name, the fixed pieces " [HP=" and "]", and the health.
feedback: toString() returns the text that stands for the object. Java then calls it for you wherever a Monster is needed as text: in println, when it is joined to a String with +, and for every element when a list is printed.

question:
Write the class Monster.
Fields (not private):  String name,  int health,  int attackPower.
A constructor  Monster(String name, int health, int attackPower)  that stores all three.
A second constructor  Monster(String name)  that gives the monster 50 health and 10 attackPower.
A method  String roar()  that returns  Dragon roars with power 50!

tests.run: Monster dragon = new Monster("Dragon", 200, 50);
Monster goblin = new Monster("Goblin");
Monster dragon = new Monster("Dragon", 200, 50);
Monster goblin = new Monster("Goblin");

Monster a = new Monster("Orc", 80, 15);
Monster b = new Monster("Slime", 10, 2);

hint: A constructor has the class's name and no return type. Two constructors are told apart by what they take in their ( ).
feedback: Fields first, then the constructors, then the method. Both constructors have the name of the class and no return type; Java chooses between them by the number of values in new Monster(…). The second can also be written in one line, this(name, 50, 10); which hands the work to the first.

question:
Write the class Weapon.
Private fields:  String name,  int damage.
A constructor  Weapon(String name, int damage).
Getters  getName()  and  getDamage().
A setter  setDamage(int newDamage).
A method  String describe()  that returns  Sword deals 25 damage.
Damage is always kept from 0 to 100: a lower value becomes 0 and a higher one becomes 100, in the constructor as well as in the setter.

tests.run: Weapon w = new Weapon("Sword", 25);
Weapon w = new Weapon("Broken Stick", -50);
Weapon w = new Weapon("God Sword", 999);

Weapon w = new Weapon("Axe", 40);
w.setDamage(60);

Weapon w = new Weapon("Bow", 20);
w.setDamage(150);

Weapon w = new Weapon("Dagger", 30);
w.setDamage(-10);

hint: The rule for damage is the same in the constructor and in the setter. The constructor may simply call setDamage(damage).
feedback: Encapsulation in one class: the fields are private, so the constructor and the setter are the only ways a damage value gets in, and both apply the same rule. Calling setDamage from the constructor keeps that rule written in one place.

question:
Write the class Hero. The class Item is given above.
Private fields:  String name,  int gold.
A constructor  Hero(String name, int gold).
Getters  getName()  and  getGold().
boolean canAfford(Item item)  is true when the hero's gold is at least the item's price.
String buyItem(Item item):  if the hero can afford it, take the price off the gold and return  Aria buys Health Potion for 20 gold.  Otherwise change nothing and return  Aria cannot afford Sword.
String status()  returns  Aria has 30 gold.

tests.run: Hero hero = new Hero("Aria", 50);

Hero hero = new Hero("Aria", 20);
Item potion = new Item("Potion", 20);

Hero hero = new Hero("Aria", 10);
Item sword = new Item("Sword", 25);

Hero hero = new Hero("Aria", 50);
Item potion = new Item("Health Potion", 20);
tests.expect: Aria buys Health Potion for 20 gold.

tests.run:
Hero hero = new Hero("Aria", 40);
hero.buyItem(new Item("Potion", 15));

hint: buyItem can call canAfford(item) to decide. An Item is asked for its details through item.getName() and item.getPrice().
feedback: One class using another through its public methods. Hero never touches Item's private fields; it asks. And buyItem leans on canAfford, a method of the same class, so the rule for “can afford” is written once.

question:
Write the class Dungeon, which keeps a list of monsters. The class Monster is given above.
Private fields:  String name,  ArrayList<Monster> monsters.
A constructor  Dungeon(String name)  that starts with an empty list.
void addMonster(Monster m)  adds a monster to the list.

hint: The constructor has to MAKE the list: monsters = new ArrayList<>(); For attackAll, do the damage in one loop and the removing in a second loop that counts down by index.
feedback: A field can be a whole collection of other objects, as long as the constructor makes the list; a field that is only declared holds no list at all. Removing inside a for-each over the same list is not allowed, which is why attackAll removes in a second loop, by index, from the end back to the start.
